questions.q: Which three services move to Kubernetes in this phase, and why those three?
options: The internal admin tools, because they're easiest to migrate first
catalog-api, checkout-api, and cart-api — the storefront path a shopper walks through during the sale
All twelve of Driftwood's services, to be thorough
The nightly reporting job and the email-notification worker, since they run on a schedule
questions.explain: catalog-api, checkout-api, and cart-api are the browse-cart-pay path customers depend on during the sale, so they're the services whose failure would fail the sale.

questions.q: What happens to the other seven services not moving to Kubernetes this phase?
options: They're decommissioned
They're explicitly deferred to a later phase, not forgotten — Lesson 20 revisits them
They're migrated anyway, just with less testing
They're merged into catalog-api
questions.explain: Good scoping means writing down what's deliberately excluded for now rather than silently dropping it; the remaining services are a real candidate list for a later phase.

questions.q: Why is the sale date the right forcing deadline for this scope, according to the lesson?
options: Because it's the only date on the calendar
Because it forces every decision to be judged against whether it will hold up under real, verified sale traffic — not just whether it's built
Because Dana Whitfield picked it at random
Because it allows unlimited scope as long as the team works overtime
questions.explain: Anchoring scope to the sale means 'finished building' and 'finished proving under real load' are treated as different milestones, which disciplines scope against creep.

questions.q: What is explicitly OUT of scope for this phase's Kubernetes migration?
options: Autoscaling checkout-api under load
Migrating the database layer itself, re-architecting service internals, and standing up a service mesh
Making catalog-api, checkout-api, and cart-api observable
Containerizing the three storefront services
questions.explain: The catalog and order data stay on their existing managed databases, no service's internal code is re-architected, and no service mesh is introduced in this phase.

questions.q: Why does this scoping lesson emphasize that this is a migration, not a greenfield build?
options: Because greenfield builds are always easier
Because the three services already run in production with real customers, which requires a parallel validated path and a real rollback option instead of a big-bang replace
Because Kubernetes doesn't support new applications
Because migrations never need rollback plans
questions.explain: Since catalog-api, checkout-api, and cart-api already serve real traffic, the migration needs a validated parallel path and a rehearsed rollback, unlike designing a new system from a blank page.
